content.text: Every Flutter frame passes through two threads with separate budgets. The UI thread runs your Dart code and produces a layer tree; the raster thread turns that tree into work for the GPU. When the raster bar is the red one, a faster

A coupons screen scrolls smoothly on the developer's phone and stutters on a budget Android device. The team spends a day on the usual advice:

constructors, smaller widgets, fewer rebuilds. Nothing changes. When someone finally opens the DevTools frames chart in profile mode, the UI bars were short all along; the tall red bars belong to the raster thread. The cause is one line repeated in every list item: each expired coupon is wrapped in
The belief: dropped frames always come from slow Dart code, usually in
means rebuilding less and computing less.
It's a fair starting point. Most performance advice is about

. Dart is the only code you write, so it feels like the only code that can be slow. And on other platforms, "don't block the main thread" covers most stutter. The half-truth: if the UI thread is the slow one, it really is your Dart code. But it's only one of two threads that must finish every frame on time.

The UI thread runs all your Dart code and the framework's: build, layout and paint. Paint doesn't produce pixels. As the docs put it, the UI thread "creates a layer tree, a lightweight object containing device-agnostic painting commands, and sends the layer tree to the raster thread to be rendered on the device." The
takes that tree and talks to the GPU; Skia and Impeller, the graphics libraries, run there. Despite the name, it runs on the CPU too.

Because the work is split, the best-practices page gives each thread its own budget: on a 60 Hz display, 16 ms for building and 16 ms for rendering. If latency matters, aim for 8 ms each, and for 120 Hz screens, under 8 ms in total. A frame that misses either budget is dropped.
Read the two graphs before you optimize

The performance overlay draws one graph per thread: the top one, labeled "GPU", is the raster thread, and the bottom one is the UI thread. The docs give the rule: a red bar in the UI graph means "the Dart code is too expensive"; a red bar in the GPU graph means "the scene is too complicated to render quickly." When both are red, start with the UI thread. The DevTools frames chart shows the same split as a pair of bars per frame.
What the raster thread pays for
You can't access the raster thread directly, but, in the docs' words, "if this thread is slow, it's a result of something you've done in the Dart code." The usual suspects, from the docs:

blocks.title: Debug mode and emulators will lie to you

content.text: Debug builds compile Dart just in time and run extra asserts, and the docs warn that JIT compilation can itself cause jank. Emulators and simulators don't use the same hardware as phones. Profile on a physical device, in profile mode, ideally the slowest one your users might reasonably own.

blocks.title: Switch effects off to find the expensive one

content.text: In the DevTools Performance view, the More debugging options menu lets you turn off rendering of clip, opacity and physical shape layers. Reproduce the stutter with one turned off: if raster time drops significantly, that effect is a likely culprit.

items.text: A frame needs both the UI thread and the raster thread to finish on time, and each has its own budget.
The UI thread runs your Dart code and produces a layer tree; the raster thread turns it into GPU work.
